11693.etyen:
Compound of E (“E”) + dur (“major”), literally “E major”.
The first element E (“E”) is the name of the musical note E. The second element dur (“major”) is via German Dur (“major”) from Middle High German bēdūre (“B-natural; hard B”), from Medieval Latin b durum (“hard B”). The adjective is from Latin dūrus (“hard”), from Proto-Italic *dūros (“hard”), from Proto-Indo-European *dweh₂rós (“long, far”), from the root *dweh₂- (“far, long”).
Compare the parallel formations Norwegian Nynorsk E-dur, Danish e-dur, Swedish E-dur, German E-Dur and Hungarian E-dúr (“E major”).

x: det er næsten for galt! – så langt mod nord – fuj!

1000365.etyen:
Onomatopoeic, originally an expressive sound associated with disgust or discomfort.
Compare the parallel expressive formations Danish fuj (“ugh, fie”), German pfui (“ugh, fie”), Dutch foei (“ugh, fie”), English fie, French fi (“fie”), Latin phui (“ugh, fie”) and Ancient Greek φεῦ (pheû, “alas”). Their exact historical relationships are uncertain because such interjections can arise independently through sound symbolism.

1000621.etyen:
Internationalism, based on Medieval Latin Croātia (“Croatia”). The Medieval Latin name is conventionally traced to Ancient Greek Χρωβατία (Khrōbatía, “Croatia”), formed from Χρωβάτος (Khrōbátos, “Croat”) and the place-name suffix -ία (-ía), literally “land of the Croats”. The ethnonym ultimately reflects Proto-Slavic *xъrvatъ (“Croat”), of uncertain deeper origin.
One modern proposal derives the ethnonym from an Iranian form meaning “guardian, protector”, but this remains disputed.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk Kroatia, Faroese Kroatia, Icelandic Króatía, Finnish Kroatia, Lithuanian Kroatija and D

a female given name from Danish

1001389.etyen:
First attested in the 18th century. Borrowed from Danish Bolette, a Danish diminutive formation based on Bol or Boel, both reduced forms of Bodil, with -ette (“diminutive suffix”). Norwegian and Danish name sources differ slightly as to whether the immediate base of Bolette was Bol or Boel.
The base name ultimately derives from Old Norse Bóthildr. The Old Norse name is a compound of bót (“remedy, help, improvement”) + hildr (“battle, fight”), literally “remedy-battle”. The The part bót (“remedy, help, improvement”) is from Proto-Germanic *bōtō (“improvement, betterment; recompense, atonement”)

1004973.etyen:
Of uncertain exact origin. Either a younger form of Old Norse Hávarr, or a variant of Håvard, from Old Norse Hávarðr.
Hávarr is traditionally analysed as a compound of hár (“high”), from Proto-Germanic *hauhaz (“high”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kewk- (“to elevate”), and a name element related to herr (“army”), from Proto-Germanic *harjaz (“army; warrior”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ker- (“army”). It may therefore be interpreted approximately as “high warrior”.
Under the alternative analysis as a variant of Håvard, see that entry for the derivation from Old Norse Hávarðr.
